title: Functions, copies and pointers
summary: Why swap(a, b) doesn't swap, and how to fix it.

cards.title: Every call gets its own box set
cards.body:
Calling a function pushes a new **stack frame**: fresh boxes for its parameters and local variables. When the function returns, the frame is thrown away.

So when you pass an `int`, the function gets a **copy**. Changing the copy changes nothing outside.
Watch the frames appear on top of main and disappear when each function returns.

cards.title: Three ways to pass
cards.body:
- `void f(int n)`: **by value**. A copy. Safe and simple for small things.
- `void f(int* n)`: **by pointer**. The function can change the caller's variable through `*n`, and n may be `nullptr`.
- `void f(int& n)`: **by reference**. Same power as a pointer, nicer syntax, never null. This is how `std::swap` works.

cards.question: What does this print?
cards.explain: bump received a copy of lives. The copy became 4 and was thrown away when bump returned.

cards.title: Build it: swap through pointers
cards.body: Write `swapValues(int* a, int* b)`. Then try changing it to take references (`int&`) and update the tests. Which do you prefer?
